assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: VSEPR model
items.clue: Predicts shapes from the repulsion between regions of electron density.

items.label: Incomplete octet
items.clue: Some atoms form stable molecules with fewer than eight valence electrons.

items.label: Allotropes
items.clue: Different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state.

items.label: Chromatography
items.clue: Separates a mixture by the different attractions of its components to two phases.

questions.stem: Ammonia, NH₃, has three bonding pairs and one lone pair around the nitrogen atom. What is its molecular geometry?

options.text: Tetrahedral, as there are four electron domains around the nitrogen atom
Trigonal planar, as only the three bonding pairs repel one another
Flat, with 90° bond angles, as the atoms are drawn in its Lewis formula on paper
Trigonal pyramidal, as the lone pair occupies one of four tetrahedral domains

questions.explanation: The four electron domains take up a tetrahedral arrangement (electron-domain geometry). Only three are occupied by atoms, so the atoms form a pyramid with N at the apex: trigonal pyramidal, with H–N–H angles of about 107°.

questions.stem: Electronegativity values: H 2.2, C 2.6, O 3.4, F 4.0, P 2.2. Which bond is the most polar?

options.text: O–H
O–F
C–F
P–H

questions.explanation: The electronegativity difference is 4.0 − 2.6 = 1.4, the largest of the four, so the shared pair is drawn most unequally, towards F.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide, CO₂, has no net dipole moment (electronegativity: C 2.6, O 3.4). Which statement explains this?

options.text: Its two C=O bond dipoles are equal and point in opposite directions, so they cancel
Its C=O bonds are non-polar, as the electronegativity difference is below 1.8
It carries no overall charge, so no separation of charge can exist in the molecule
Its carbon atom has no lone pair, and only lone pairs can produce a net dipole

questions.explanation: Each C=O bond is polar (difference 0.8, δ− on O). Carbon has two electron domains, so the molecule is linear and the two equal bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions. Their vector sum is zero.

questions.stem: Predict the H–O–H bond angle in a water molecule, H₂O.

options.text: About 104.5°, as lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs do
About 109.5°, as all four electron domains around O repel one another equally
About 180°, as the two bonding pairs get as far apart as possible
About 90°, as the H atoms are drawn at right angles in its Lewis formula

questions.explanation: Oxygen has four electron domains (two bonding pairs, two lone pairs) in a tetrahedral arrangement. The two lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, squeezing the H–O–H angle below 109.5° to about 104.5°.

questions.stem: Electronegativity values: H 2.2, N 3.0. Which statement describes the N–H bond in ammonia, NH₃?

options.text: Each hydrogen atom has given its electron to nitrogen, so N³⁻ and H⁺ ions attract
The pair is shared equally, because a difference of 0.8 is too small to make a bond polar
Both atoms gain a share of the pair, so nitrogen and hydrogen are both δ−
The shared pair lies closer to nitrogen, so nitrogen is δ− and hydrogen is δ+

questions.explanation: Nitrogen (3.0) attracts the shared pair more strongly than hydrogen (2.2). Electron density shifts towards nitrogen, which carries a partial negative charge, δ−, leaving hydrogen with an equal partial positive charge, δ+.

questions.stem: Water, H₂O, has a net dipole moment (electronegativity: H 2.2, O 3.4). Which statement explains this?

options.text: Its O–H bonds are polar, and every molecule with polar bonds has a net dipole
It is bent, so its two O–H bond dipoles do not point in opposite directions
Its H atoms lie at 90° to each other, as in its Lewis formula, so the dipoles add
Its oxygen atom has two lone pairs, which are the only source of its net dipole

questions.explanation: Each O–H bond is polar (δ− on O). Oxygen's four electron domains (two of them lone pairs) make the molecule bent, about 104.5°, so the two bond dipoles add to give a resultant along the bisector of the angle.

questions.stem: In methanal, H₂CO, the carbon atom forms a single bond to each of two hydrogen atoms and a double bond to the oxygen atom. What is the best prediction of the H–C–H bond angle?

options.text: About 109.5°, as the two bonds of C=O count as two separate electron domains
Slightly less than 120°, as the C=O double bond repels more than a single bond
Exactly 120°, as all three electron domains around carbon repel equally
About 104.5°, as oxygen's two lone pairs push the two C–H bonds together

questions.explanation: Carbon has three electron domains (two C–H bonds and the C=O bond), so the arrangement is trigonal planar. The double bond holds more electron density and repels the C–H bonds more strongly, so the H–C–H angle is squeezed slightly below 120° (to about 116°).
